1|Configuration & API
2|===================
3|
4|Noxfile
5|-------
6|
7|Nox looks for configuration in a file named ``noxfile.py`` by default. You can specify
8|a different file using the ``--noxfile`` argument when running ``nox``.
9|
10|
11|Defining sessions
12|-----------------
13|
14|.. autofunction:: nox.session
15|
16|Nox sessions are configured via standard Python functions that are decorated
17|with ``@nox.session``. For example:
18|
19|.. code-block:: python
20|
21|    import nox
22|
23|    @nox.session
24|    def tests(session):
25|        session.run('pytest')
26|
27|You can also configure sessions to run against multiple Python versions as described in :ref:`virtualenv config` and  parametrize sessions as described in :ref:`parametrized sessions <parametrized>`.
28|
29|By default, all sessions will be run if no sessions are specified. You can
30|remove sessions from this default list by passing ``default=False`` in the
31|``@nox.session(...)`` decorator. You can also specify a list of sessions to run by
32|default using the ``nox.options.sessions = [...]`` configuration option.
33|
34|Session description
35|-------------------
36|
37|You can add a description to your session using a `docstring <https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0257>`__.
38|The first line will be shown when listing the sessions. For example:
39|
40|.. code-block:: python
41|
42|    import nox
43|
44|    @nox.session
45|    def tests(session):
46|        """Run the test suite."""
47|        session.run('pytest')
48|
49|The ``nox --list`` command will show:
50|
51|.. code-block:: console
52|
53|    $ nox --list
54|    Available sessions:
55|    * tests -> Run the test suite.
56|
57|The ``--list`` command shows the first line of the docstring as the session's description. You can also
58|show the full docstring of a session using the ``--usage`` option, especially if it has multiple lines.
59|For example:
60|
61|.. code-block:: console
62|
63|    $ nox --usage tests
64|    Run the test suite.
65|
66|    The test suite consists of all tests in tests/.
67|
68|
69|Session name
70|------------
71|
72|By default Nox uses the decorated function's name as the session name. This works wonderfully for the vast majority of projects, however, if you need to you can customize the session's name by using the ``name`` argument to ``@nox.session``. For example:
73|
74|.. code-block:: python
75|
76|    import nox
77|
78|    @nox.session(name="custom-name")
79|    def a_very_long_function_name(session):
80|        print("Hello!")
81|
82|
83|The ``nox --list`` command will show:
84|
85|.. code-block:: console
86|
87|    $ nox --list
88|    Available sessions:
89|    * custom-name
90|
91|And you can tell ``nox`` to run the session using the custom name:
92|
93|.. code-block:: console
94|
95|    $ nox --session "custom-name"
96|    Hello!
97|
98|
99|.. _virtualenv config:
100|
101|Configuring a session's virtualenv
102|----------------------------------
103|
104|By default, Nox will create a new virtualenv for each session using the same interpreter that Nox uses. If you installed Nox using Python 3.12, Nox will use Python 3.12 by default for all of your sessions.
105|
106|You can tell Nox to use a different Python interpreter/version by specifying the ``python`` argument (or its alias ``py``) to ``@nox.session``:
107|
108|.. code-block:: python
109|
110|    @nox.session(python='3.12')
111|    def tests(session):
112|        pass
113|
114|.. note::
115|
116|    Interpreters are located with the `python-discovery`_ library, which searches
117|    ``PATH``, version managers (pyenv, mise, asdf, uv), and, on Windows, the
118|    registry (`PEP 514`_) and the Python `Launcher`_. If a given test needs to use
119|    the 32-bit version of a given Python on Windows, then ``X.Y-32`` should be used
120|    as the version.
121|
122|    .. _Launcher: https://docs.python.org/3/using/windows.html#python-launcher-for-windows
123|    .. _python-discovery: https://pypi.org/project/python-discovery/
124|    .. _PEP 514: https://peps.python.org/pep-0514/
125|
126|Nox does not impose a separate supported-version range on the Python
127|interpreters used by sessions. A target version works when Nox can discover or
128|download its interpreter and the selected environment backend can create an
129|environment with it. Backends and the packages they use may have their own
130|Python support ranges. Any non end-of-life Python should work, and
131|a few older Python versions usually work too depending on the backend.
132|
133|You can also tell Nox to run your session against multiple Python interpreters. Nox will create a separate virtualenv and run the session for each interpreter you specify. For example, this session will run twice - once for Python 3.13 and once for Python 3.14:
134|
135|.. code-block:: python
136|
137|    @nox.session(python=['3.13', '3.14'])
138|    def tests(session):
139|        pass
140|
141|When you provide a version number, Nox automatically prepends python to determine the name of the executable. However, Nox also accepts the full executable name. If you want to test using pypy, for example:
142|
143|.. code-block:: python
144|
145|    @nox.session(python=['3.13', '3.14', 'pypy3.11'])
146|    def tests(session):
147|        pass
148|
149|A free-threaded build can be requested with the ``t`` suffix, e.g. ``python='3.13t'``.
150|
151|You can also give a `PEP 440`_ version specifier instead of an exact version, and
152|Nox will use the first installed interpreter that satisfies it:
153|
154|.. code-block:: python
155|
156|    @nox.session(python='>=3.14')
157|    def tests(session):
158|        pass
159|
160|    @nox.session(python='>=3.11,<3.13')
161|    def lint(session):
162|        pass
163|
164|.. note::
165|
166|    Range specifiers are only supported on the ``venv``, ``virtualenv``, and ``uv``
167|    backends, not on conda backends.
168|
169|If the specified python interpreter is not found, Nox can automatically download it when ``--download-python`` is set to ``auto`` (the default) or ``always``. ``never`` avoids the download. This requires the ``[pbs]`` extra when not using uv as a backend. When a range is given, the floor of its lowest bound is downloaded (``>=3.14`` downloads ``3.14``). A range with only upper bounds downloads the highest minor version that the range fully allows (``<3.14`` downloads ``3.13``, ``<=3.14.4`` downloads ``3.13``, ``<3.14,!=3.13.*`` downloads ``3.12``). A range with no usable bound (such as ``!=3.12``) cannot be downloaded.
170|
171|When collecting your sessions, Nox will create a separate session for each interpreter. You can see these sessions when running ``nox --list``. For example this Noxfile:
172|
173|.. code-block:: python
174|
175|    @nox.session(python=['3.10', '3.11', '3.12', '3.13', '3.14'])
176|    def tests(session):
177|        pass
178|
179|Will produce these sessions:
180|
181|.. code-block:: console
182|
183|    * tests-3.10
184|    * tests-3.11
185|    * tests-3.12
186|    * tests-3.13
187|    * tests-3.14
188|
189|Note that this expansion happens *before* parameterization occurs, so you can still parametrize sessions with multiple interpreters.
190|
191|If you want to disable virtualenv creation altogether, you can set ``python`` to ``False``, or set ``venv_backend`` to ``"none"``, both are equivalent. Note that this can be done temporarily through the :ref:`--no-venv <opt-force-venv-backend>` commandline flag, too.
192|
193|.. code-block:: python
194|
195|    @nox.session(python=False)
196|    def tests(session):
197|        pass
198|
199|Use of :func:`session.install()` is deprecated without a virtualenv since it modifies the global Python environment. If this is what you really want, use :func:`session.run()` and pip instead.
200|
201|.. code-block:: python
202|
203|    @nox.session(python=False)
204|    def tests(session):
205|        session.run("pip", "install", "nox")
206|
207|You can also specify that the virtualenv should *always* be reused instead of recreated every time unless ``--reuse-venv=never``:
208|
209|.. code-block:: python
210|
211|    @nox.session(
212|        python=['3.13', '3.14'],
213|        reuse_venv=True)
214|    def tests(session):
215|        pass
216|
217|You are not limited to virtualenv, there is a selection of backends you can choose from as venv, uv, conda, mamba, micromamba, rattler, or virtualenv (default):
218|
219|.. code-block:: python
220|
221|    @nox.session(venv_backend='venv')
222|    def tests(session):
223|        pass
224|
225|You can chain together optional backends with ``|``, such as ``uv|virtualenv``
226|or ``rattler|micromamba|mamba|conda``, and the first available backend will be selected.
227|You cannot put anything after a backend that can't be missing like ``venv`` or
228|``virtualenv``.
229|
230|.. tip::
231|
232|    If a session targets an end-of-life Python version while Nox itself runs on
233|    a newer Python, prefer the ``venv`` backend for that session. The
234|    ``virtualenv`` backend runs from Nox's interpreter and may no longer support
235|    bootstrapping older target interpreters after they reach end of life, which
236|    can seed incompatible packages into the session environment. The ``venv``
237|    backend uses the target interpreter's standard library ``venv`` module
238|    instead.
239|
240|    .. code-block:: python
241|
242|        @nox.session(python='3.7', venv_backend='venv')
243|        def tests(session):
244|            pass
245|
246|Finally, custom backend parameters are supported:
247|
248|.. code-block:: python
249|
250|    @nox.session(venv_params=['--no-download'])
251|    def tests(session):
252|        pass
253|
254|If you need to check to see which backend was selected, you can access it via
255|``session.venv_backend``.
256|
257|
258|Passing arguments into sessions
259|-------------------------------
260|
261|Often it's useful to pass arguments into your test session. Here's a quick
262|example that demonstrates how to use arguments to run tests against a
263|particular file:
264|
265|.. code-block:: python
266|
267|    @nox.session
268|    def test(session):
269|        session.install('pytest')
270|
271|        if session.posargs:
272|            test_files = session.posargs
273|        else:
274|            test_files = ['test_a.py', 'test_b.py']
275|
276|        session.run('pytest', *test_files)
277|
278|Now if you run:
279|
280|
281|.. code-block:: console
282|
283|    nox
284|
285|
286|Then nox will run:
287|
288|.. code-block:: console
289|
290|    pytest test_a.py test_b.py
291|
292|
293|But if you run:
294|
295|.. code-block:: console
296|
297|    nox -- test_c.py
298|
299|
300|Then nox will run:
301|
302|.. code-block:: console
303|
304|    pytest test_c.py
305|
306|
307|.. _parametrized:
308|
309|Parametrizing sessions
310|----------------------
311|
312|Session arguments can be parametrized with the :func:`nox.parametrize` decorator. Here's a typical example of parametrizing the Django version to install:
313|
314|.. code-block:: python
315|
316|    @nox.session
317|    @nox.parametrize('django', ['1.9', '2.0'])
318|    def tests(session, django):
319|        session.install(f'django=={django}')
320|        session.run('pytest')
321|
322|When you run ``nox``, it will create two distinct sessions:
323|
324|.. code-block:: console
325|
326|    $ nox
327|    nox > Running session tests(django='1.9')
328|    nox > python -m pip install django==1.9
329|    ...
330|    nox > Running session tests(django='2.0')
331|    nox > python -m pip install django==2.0
332|
333|
334|:func:`nox.parametrize` has an interface and usage intentionally similar to `pytest's parametrize <https://pytest.org/latest/parametrize.html#_pytest.python.Metafunc.parametrize>`_.
335|
336|.. autofunction:: nox.parametrize
337|
338|You can also stack the decorator to produce sessions that are a combination of the arguments, for example:
339|
340|.. code-block:: python
341|
342|    @nox.session
343|    @nox.parametrize('django', ['1.9', '2.0'])
344|    @nox.parametrize('database', ['postgres', 'mysql'])
345|    def tests(session, django, database):
346|        ...
347|
348|
349|If you run ``nox --list``, you'll see that this generates the following set of sessions:
350|
351|.. code-block:: console
352|
353|    * tests(database='postgres', django='1.9')
354|    * tests(database='mysql', django='1.9')
355|    * tests(database='postgres', django='2.0')
356|    * tests(database='mysql', django='2.0')
357|
358|
359|If you only want to run one of the parametrized sessions, see :ref:`running_paramed_sessions`.
360|
361|
362|Giving friendly names to parametrized sessions
363|----------------------------------------------
364|
365|The automatically generated names for parametrized sessions, such as ``tests(django='1.9', database='postgres')``, can be long and unwieldy to work with even with using :ref:`keyword filtering <opt-sessions-pythons-and-keywords>`. You can give parametrized sessions custom IDs to help in this scenario. These two examples are equivalent:
366|
367|.. code-block:: python
368|
369|    @nox.session
370|    @nox.parametrize('django',
371|        ['1.9', '2.0'],
372|        ids=['old', 'new'])
373|    def tests(session, django):
374|        ...
375|
376|.. code-block:: python
377|
378|    @nox.session
379|    @nox.parametrize('django', [
380|        nox.param('1.9', id='old'),
381|        nox.param('2.0', id='new'),
382|    ])
383|    def tests(session, django):
384|        ...
385|
386|When running ``nox --list`` you'll see their new IDs:
387|
388|.. code-block:: console
389|
390|    * tests(old)
391|    * tests(new)
392|
393|And you can run them with ``nox --sessions "tests(old)"`` and so on.
394|
395|This works with stacked parameterizations as well. The IDs are combined during the combination. For example:
396|
397|.. code-block:: python
398|
399|    @nox.session
400|    @nox.parametrize(
401|        'django',
402|        ['1.9', '2.0'],
403|        ids=["old", "new"])
404|    @nox.parametrize(
405|        'database',
406|        ['postgres', 'mysql'],
407|        ids=["psql", "mysql"])
408|    def tests(session, django, database):
409|        ...
410|
411|Produces these sessions when running ``nox --list``:
412|
413|.. code-block:: console
414|
415|    * tests(psql, old)
416|    * tests(mysql, old)
417|    * tests(psql, new)
418|    * tests(mysql, new)
419|
420|
421|Parametrizing the session Python
422|--------------------------------
423|
424|You can use parametrization to select the Python interpreter for a session.
425|These two examples are equivalent:
426|
427|.. code-block:: python
428|
429|    @nox.session
430|    @nox.parametrize("python", ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12"])
431|    def tests(session):
432|        ...
433|
434|    @nox.session(python=["3.10", "3.11", "3.12"])
435|    def tests(session):
436|        ...
437|
438|The first form can be useful if you need to exclude some combinations of Python
439|versions with other parameters. For example, you may want to test against
440|multiple versions of a dependency, but the latest version doesn't run on older
441|Pythons:
442|
443|.. code-block:: python
444|
445|    @nox.session
446|    @nox.parametrize(
447|        "python,dependency",
448|        [
449|            (python, dependency)
450|            for python in ("3.10", "3.11", "3.12")
451|            for dependency in ("1.0", "2.0")
452|            if (python, dependency) != ("3.10", "2.0")
453|        ],
454|    )
455|    def tests(session, dependency):
456|        ...
457|
458|
459|Assigning tags to parametrized sessions
460|---------------------------------------
461|
462|Just as tags can be :ref:`assigned to normal sessions <session tags>`, they can also be assigned to parametrized sessions.  The following examples are both equivalent:
463|
464|.. code-block:: python
465|
466|    @nox.session
467|    @nox.parametrize('dependency',
468|        ['1.0', '2.0'],
469|        tags=[['old'], ['new']])
470|    @nox.parametrize('database',
471|        ['postgres', 'mysql'],
472|        tags=[['psql'], ['mysql']])
473|    def tests(session, dependency, database):
474|        ...
475|
476|.. code-block:: python
477|
478|    @nox.session
479|    @nox.parametrize('dependency', [
480|        nox.param('1.0', tags=['old']),
481|        nox.param('2.0', tags=['new']),
482|    ])
483|    @nox.parametrize('database', [
484|        nox.param('postgres', tags=['psql']),
485|        nox.param('mysql', tags=['mysql']),
486|    ])
487|    def tests(session, dependency, database):
488|        ...
489|
490|In either case, running ``nox --tags old`` will run the tests using version 1.0 of the dependency against both database backends, while running ``nox --tags psql`` will run the tests using both versions of the dependency, but only against PostgreSQL.
491|
492|More sophisticated tag assignment can be performed by passing a generator to the ``@nox.parametrize`` decorator, as seen in the following example:
493|
494|.. code-block:: python
495|
496|    def generate_params():
497|        for dependency in ["1.0", "1.1", "2.0"]:
498|            for database in ["sqlite", "postgresql", "mysql"]:
499|                tags = []
500|                if dependency == "2.0" and database == "sqlite":
501|                    tags.append("quick")
502|                if dependency == "2.0" or database == "sqlite":
503|                    tags.append("standard")
504|                yield nox.param(dependency, database, tags=tags)
505|
506|    @nox.session
507|    @nox.parametrize(["dependency", "database"], generate_params())
508|    def tests(session, dependency, database):
509|        ...
510|
511|In this example, the ``quick`` tag is assigned to the single combination of the latest version of the dependency along with the SQLite database backend, allowing a developer to run the tests in a single configuration as a basic sanity test.  The ``standard`` tag, in contrast, selects combinations targeting either the latest version of the dependency *or* the SQLite database backend.  If the developer runs ``nox --tags standard``, the tests will be run against all supported versions of the dependency with the SQLite backend, as well as against all supported database backends under the latest version of the dependency, giving much more comprehensive test coverage while using only five of the potential nine test matrix combinations.
512|
513|
514|The session object
515|------------------
516|
517|.. module:: nox.sessions
518|
519|Nox will call your session functions with an instance of the :class:`Session`
520|class.
521|
522|Use :attr:`Session.parallel` to detect execution under Nox's parallel
523|scheduler and avoid enabling another layer of automatic parallelism:
524|
525|.. code-block:: python
526|
527|    @nox.session(allow_parallel=True)
528|    def tests(session):
529|        session.install("pytest", "pytest-xdist")
530|        session.run("pytest", "-n", "0" if session.parallel else "auto")
531|
532|.. autoclass:: Session
533|    :members:
534|    :undoc-members:
535|
536|The pyproject.toml helpers
537|--------------------------
538|
539|Nox provides helpers for ``pyproject.toml`` projects in the ``nox.project`` namespace.
540|
541|.. automodule:: nox.project
542|   :members:
543|
544|Modifying Nox's behavior in the Noxfile
545|---------------------------------------
546|
547|Nox has various :doc:`command line arguments <usage>` that can be used to modify its behavior. Some of these can also be specified in the Noxfile using ``nox.options``. For example, if you wanted to store Nox's virtualenvs in a different directory without needing to pass it into ``nox`` every time:
548|
549|.. code-block:: python
550|
551|    import nox
552|
553|    nox.options.envdir = ".cache"
554|
555|    @nox.session
556|    def tests(session):
557|        ...
558|
559|Or, if you wanted to provide a set of sessions that are run by default (this overrides the ``default=`` argument to sessions):
560|
561|.. code-block:: python
562|
563|    import nox
564|
565|    nox.options.sessions = ["lint", "tests-3.14"]
566|
567|    ...
568|
569|The following options can be specified in the Noxfile:
570|
571|* ``nox.options.envdir`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`--envdir <opt-envdir>`.
572|* ``nox.options.sessions`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`-s or --sessions <opt-sessions-pythons-and-keywords>`. If set to an empty list, no sessions will be run if no sessions were given on the command line, and the list of available sessions will be shown instead.
573|* ``nox.options.pythons`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`-p or --pythons <opt-sessions-pythons-and-keywords>`.
574|* ``nox.options.keywords`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`-k or --keywords <opt-sessions-pythons-and-keywords>`.
575|* ``nox.options.tags`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`-t or --tags <opt-sessions-pythons-and-keywords>`.
576|* ``nox.options.default_venv_backend`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`-db or --default-venv-backend <opt-default-venv-backend>`.
577|* ``nox.options.force_venv_backend`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`-fb or --force-venv-backend <opt-force-venv-backend>`.
578|* ``nox.options.reuse_venv`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`--reuse-venv <opt-reuse-venv>`. Preferred over using ``nox.options.reuse_existing_virtualenvs``.
579|* ``nox.options.reuse_existing_virtualenvs`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`--reuse-existing-virtualenvs <opt-reuse-existing-virtualenvs>`. You can force this off by specifying ``--no-reuse-existing-virtualenvs`` during invocation. Alias of ``nox.options.reuse_venv=yes|no``.
580|* ``nox.options.stop_on_first_error`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`--stop-on-first-error <opt-stop-on-first-error>`. You can force this off by specifying ``--no-stop-on-first-error`` during invocation.
581|* ``nox.options.error_on_missing_interpreters`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`--error-on-missing-interpreters <opt-error-on-missing-interpreters>`. You can force this off by specifying ``--no-error-on-missing-interpreters`` during invocation.
582|* ``nox.options.error_on_external_run`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`--error-on-external-run <opt-error-on-external-run>`. You can force this off by specifying ``--no-error-on-external-run`` during invocation.
583|* ``nox.options.download_python`` is equivalent to specifying ``--download-python``.
584|* ``nox.options.parallel`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`-j or --parallel <opt-parallel>`.
585|* ``nox.options.allow_parallel`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`--allow-parallel <opt-allow-parallel>`. You can force this off by specifying ``--no-allow-parallel`` during invocation.
586|* ``nox.options.report`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`--report <opt-report>`.
587|* ``nox.options.verbose`` is equivalent to specifying :ref:`-v or --verbose <opt-verbose>`. You can force this off by specifying ``--no-verbose`` during invocation.
588|
589|
590|When invoking ``nox``, any options specified on the command line take precedence over the options specified in the Noxfile. If either ``--sessions`` or ``--keywords`` is specified on the command line, *both* options specified in the Noxfile will be ignored.
591|
592|
593|Nox version requirements
594|------------------------
595|
596|Nox version requirements can be specified in your Noxfile by setting
597|``nox.needs_version``. If the Nox version does not satisfy the requirements, Nox
598|exits with a friendly error message. For example:
599|
600|.. code-block:: python
601|
602|    import nox
603|
604|    nox.needs_version = ">=2019.5.30"
605|
606|    @nox.session(name="test")  # name argument was added in 2019.5.30
607|    def pytest(session):
608|        session.run("pytest")
609|
610|Any of the version specifiers defined in `PEP 440`_ can be used.
611|
612|.. warning:: Version requirements *must* be specified as a string literal,
613|    using a simple assignment to ``nox.needs_version`` at the module level. This
614|    allows Nox to check the version without importing the Noxfile.
615|
616|.. _PEP 440: https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0440/

1|Command-line usage
2|==================
3|
4|Invocation
5|----------
6|
7|Nox is normally invoked on the command line:
8|
9|.. code-block:: console
10|
11|    nox
12|
13|
14|You can also invoke Nox via the Python interpreter:
15|
16|.. code-block:: console
17|
18|    python3 -m nox
19|
20|
21|Listing available sessions
22|--------------------------
23|
24|To list all available sessions, including parametrized sessions:
25|
26|
27|.. code-block:: console
28|
29|    nox -l
30|    nox --list
31|    nox --list-sessions
32|
33|If you'd like to use the output in later processing, you can add ``--json`` to
34|get json output for the selected session. Fields include ``session`` (pretty
35|name), ``name``, ``description``, ``python`` (null if not specified), ``tags``,
36|and ``call_spec`` (for parametrized sessions).
37|
38|To get more information about one particular session at a time, you can use ``--usage``:
39|
40|.. code-block:: console
41|
42|    nox --usage tests
43|
44|.. _session_execution_order:
45|
46|Running all sessions
47|--------------------
48|
49|You can run every session by just executing ``nox`` without any arguments:
50|
51|.. code-block:: console
52|
53|    nox
54|
55|The order that sessions are executed is the order that they appear in the Noxfile.
56|
57|
58|.. _opt-sessions-pythons-and-keywords:
59|
60|Specifying one or more sessions
61|-------------------------------
62|
63|By default Nox will run all sessions defined in the Noxfile. However, you can choose to run a particular set of them using ``--session``, ``-s``, or ``-e``:
64|
65|.. tabs::
66|
67|   .. code-tab:: console CLI options
68|
69|         nox --session tests
70|         nox -s lint tests
71|         nox -e lint
72|
73|   .. code-tab:: console Environment variables
74|
75|         NOXSESSION=tests nox
76|         NOXSESSION=lint nox
77|         NOXSESSION=lint,tests nox
78|
79|Nox will run these sessions in the same order they are specified.
80|
81|If you have a :ref:`configured session's virtualenv <virtualenv config>`, you can choose to run only sessions with given Python versions:
82|
83|.. tabs::
84|
85|   .. code-tab:: console CLI options
86|
87|         nox --python 3.12
88|         nox -p 3.11 3.12
89|
90|   .. code-tab:: console Environment variables
91|
92|         NOXPYTHON=3.12 nox
93|         NOXPYTHON=3.11,3.12 nox
94|
95|You can also use `pytest-style keywords`_ using ``-k`` or ``--keywords``, and
96|tags using ``-t`` or ``--tags`` to filter test sessions:
97|
98|.. code-block:: console
99|
100|    nox -k "not lint"
101|    nox -k "tests and not lint"
102|    nox -k "not my_tag"
103|    nox -t "my_tag" "my_other_tag"
104|
105|.. _pytest-style keywords: https://docs.pytest.org/en/latest/usage.html#specifying-tests-selecting-tests
106|
107|
108|.. _running_paramed_sessions:
109|
110|Specifying parametrized sessions
111|--------------------------------
112|
113|If you have a :ref:`parametrized <parametrized>` session such as:
114|
115|.. code-block:: python
116|
117|    @nox.parametrize('django', ['1.9', '2.0'])
118|    def tests(session, django):
119|        ...
120|
121|Then running ``nox --session tests`` will actually run all parametrized versions of the session. If you want the run the session with a particular set of parametrized arguments, you can specify them with the session name:
122|
123|.. code-block:: console
124|
125|    nox --session "tests(django='1.9')"
126|    nox --session "tests(django='2.0')"
127|
128|
129|.. _opt-default-venv-backend:
130|
131|Changing the sessions default backend
132|-------------------------------------
133|
134|By default Nox uses ``virtualenv`` as the virtual environment backend for the sessions, but it also supports ``uv``, ``conda``, ``mamba``, ``micromamba``, ``rattler``, and ``venv`` as well as no backend (passthrough to whatever python environment Nox is running on). You can change the default behaviour by using ``-db <backend>`` or ``--default-venv-backend <backend>``. Supported names are ``('none', 'uv', 'virtualenv', 'conda', 'mamba', 'micromamba', 'rattler', 'venv')``.
135|
136|
137|.. tabs::
138|
139|   .. code-tab:: console CLI options
140|
141|         nox -db conda
142|         nox --default-venv-backend conda
143|
144|   .. code-tab:: console Environment variables
145|
146|         NOX_DEFAULT_VENV_BACKEND=conda
147|
148|.. note::
149|
150|   The ``uv``, ``conda``, ``mamba``, and ``micromamba`` backends require their
151|   respective programs be pre-installed. ``uv`` is distributed as a Python
152|   package and can be installed with the ``nox[uv]`` extra.
153|
154|   The ``rattler`` backend creates conda environments with `py-rattler
155|   <https://github.com/conda/rattler>`_ without needing an installed CLI.
156|   Install it with the ``nox[rattler]`` extra; in script mode, list
157|   ``nox[rattler]`` in the script dependencies. It solves from ``conda-forge``
158|   unless ``venv_params`` sets ``--channel``. :meth:`session.conda_install
159|   <nox.sessions.Session.conda_install>` accepts specs, ``--channel`` and
160|   ``--file`` only.
161|
162|You can also set this option with the ``NOX_DEFAULT_VENV_BACKEND`` environment variable, or in the Noxfile with ``nox.options.default_venv_backend``. In case more than one is provided, the command line argument overrides the environment variable, which in turn overrides the Noxfile configuration.
163|
164|Note that using this option does not change the backend for sessions where ``venv_backend`` is explicitly set.
165|
166|.. warning::
167|
168|   The ``uv`` backend does not install anything by default, including ``pip``,
169|   as ``uv pip`` is used to install programs instead. If you need to manually
170|   interact with pip, you should install it with ``session.install("pip")``.
171|
172|Backends that could be missing (``uv``, ``conda``, ``mamba``, ``micromamba``, and ``rattler``) can have a fallback using ``|``, such as ``uv|virtualenv`` or ``micromamba|mamba|conda``. This will use the first item that is available on the users system.
173|
174|If you need to check to see which backend was selected, you can access it via
175|``session.venv_backend`` in your noxfile.
176|
177|.. _opt-force-venv-backend:
178|
179|Forcing the sessions backend
180|----------------------------
181|
182|You might work in a different environment than a project's default continuous integration settings, and might wish to get a quick way to execute the same tasks but on a different venv backend. For this purpose, you can temporarily force the backend used by **all** sessions in the current Nox execution by using ``-fb <backend>`` or ``--force-venv-backend <backend>``. No exceptions are made, the backend will be forced for all sessions run whatever the other options values and Noxfile configuration. Supported names are ``('none', 'uv', 'virtualenv', 'conda', 'mamba', 'micromamba', 'rattler', 'venv')``.
183|
184|.. code-block:: console
185|
186|    nox -fb conda
187|    nox --force-venv-backend conda
188|
189|
190|You can also set this option in the Noxfile with ``nox.options.force_venv_backend``. In case both are provided, the commandline argument takes precedence.
191|
192|Finally note that the ``--no-venv`` flag is a shortcut for ``--force-venv-backend none`` and allows to temporarily run all selected sessions on the current python interpreter (the one running Nox).
193|
194|.. code-block:: console
195|
196|    nox --no-venv
197|
198|.. _opt-reuse-existing-virtualenvs:
199|.. _opt-reuse-venv:
200|
201|Reusing virtualenvs
202|-------------------
203|
204|By default, Nox deletes and recreates virtualenvs every time it is run. This is
205|usually fine for most projects and continuous integration environments as
206|`pip's caching <https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/cli/pip_install/#caching>`_ makes
207|re-install rather quick.  However, there are some situations where it is
208|advantageous to reuse the virtualenvs between runs.  Use ``-r`` or
209|``--reuse-existing-virtualenvs`` or for fine-grained control use
210|``--reuse-venv=yes|no|always|never``:
211|
212|.. code-block:: console
213|
214|    nox -r
215|    nox --reuse-existing-virtualenvs
216|    nox --reuse-venv=yes # preferred
217|
218|If the Noxfile sets ``nox.options.reuse_existing_virtualenvs``, you can override the Noxfile setting from the command line by using ``--no-reuse-existing-virtualenvs``.
219|Similarly you can override ``nox.options.reuse_venvs`` from the Noxfile via the command line by using ``--reuse-venv=yes|no|always|never``.
220|
221|.. note::
222|
223|    ``--reuse-existing-virtualenvs`` is an alias for ``--reuse-venv=yes`` and ``--no-reuse-existing-virtualenvs`` is an alias for ``--reuse-venv=no``.
224|
225|Additionally, you can skip the re-installation of packages when a virtualenv is reused.
226|Use ``-R`` or ``--reuse-existing-virtualenvs --no-install`` or ``--reuse-venv=yes --no-install``:
227|
228|.. code-block:: console
229|
230|    nox -R
231|    nox --reuse-existing-virtualenvs --no-install
232|    nox --reuse-venv=yes --no-install
233|
234|The ``--no-install`` option causes the following session methods to return early:
235|
236|- :func:`session.install <nox.sessions.Session.install>`
237|- :func:`session.conda_install <nox.sessions.Session.conda_install>`
238|- :func:`session.run_install <nox.sessions.Session.run_install>`
239|
240|The ``never`` and ``always`` options in ``--reuse-venv`` gives you more fine-grained control
241|as it ignores when a ``@nox.session`` has ``reuse_venv=True|False`` defined.
242|
243|These options have no effect if the virtualenv is not being reused.
244|
245|.. _opt-running-extra-pythons:
246|
247|Running additional Python versions
248|----------------------------------
249|
250|In addition to Nox supporting executing single sessions, it also supports running Python versions that aren't specified using ``--extra-pythons``.
251|
252|.. tabs::
253|
254|   .. code-tab:: console CLI options
255|
256|         nox --extra-pythons 3.12 3.13 3.14
257|
258|   .. code-tab:: console Environment variables
259|
260|         NOXEXTRAPYTHON=3.12,3.13,3.14 nox
261|
262|
263|This will, in addition to specified Python versions in the Noxfile, also create sessions for the specified versions.
264|
265|This option can be combined with ``--python`` to replace, instead of appending, the Python interpreter for a given session:
266|
267|.. tabs::
268|
269|   .. code-tab:: console CLI options
270|
271|         nox --python 3.11 --extra-python 3.11 -s lint
272|
273|   .. code-tab:: console Environment variables
274|
275|         NOXPYTHON=3.11 NOXEXTRAPYTHON=3.11 NOXSESSION=lint nox
276|
277|Instead of passing both options, you can use the ``--force-python`` shorthand:
278|
279|.. tabs::
280|
281|   .. code-tab:: console CLI options
282|
283|         nox --force-python 3.11 -s lint
284|
285|   .. code-tab:: console Environment variables
286|
287|         NOXFORCEPYTHON=3.11 NOXSESSION=lint nox
288|
289|Also, you can specify ``python`` in place of a specific version. This will run the session
290|using the ``python`` specified for the current ``PATH``:
291|
292|.. tabs::
293|
294|   .. code-tab:: console CLI options
295|
296|         nox --force-python python -s lint
297|
298|   .. code-tab:: console Environment variables
299|
300|         NOXFORCEPYTHON=python NOXSESSION=lint nox
301|
302|Downloading Python interpreters
303|-------------------------------
304|
305|Nox can download Python interpreters, either via uv or directly from
306|python-build-standalone (requires the ``[pbs]`` extra), by using
307|``--download-python``:
308|
309|.. code-block:: console
310|
311|    nox --download-python auto    # Download if interpreter not found (default)
312|    nox --download-python never   # Never download interpreters
313|    nox --download-python always  # Always download interpreters
314|
315|You can also set this option with the ``NOX_DOWNLOAD_PYTHON`` environment
316|variable.
317|
318|.. _opt-stop-on-first-error:
319|
320|Stopping if any session fails
321|-----------------------------
322|
323|By default Nox will continue to run all sessions even if one fails. You can use ``--stop-on-first-error`` to make Nox abort as soon as the first session fails::
324|
325|    nox --stop-on-first-error
326|
327|If the Noxfile sets ``nox.options.stop_on_first_error``, you can override the Noxfile setting from the command line by using ``--no-stop-on-first-error``.
328|
329|
330|.. _opt-parallel:
331|
332|Running sessions in parallel
333|----------------------------
334|
335|By default Nox runs sessions one at a time. Use ``-j`` / ``--parallel`` to run
336|independent sessions concurrently, each in its own subprocess::
337|
338|    nox --parallel auto   # one session per CPU
339|    nox -j 4              # at most four sessions at once
340|
341|The value is a positive integer or ``auto`` (the number of CPUs). The default
342|is ``1`` (sequential). The environment variable ``NOX_PARALLEL`` and
343|``nox.options.parallel`` in the Noxfile are also honored.
344|
345|Parallel execution is opt-in per session: only sessions declared with
346|``allow_parallel=True`` may run at the same time::
347|
348|    @nox.session(allow_parallel=True)
349|    def tests(session):
350|        ...
351|
352|Sessions that don't opt in still run under ``--parallel``, but not in parallel.
353|They start only once nothing else is running, and nothing starts alongside
354|them. If no selected session opts in, Nox warns and runs sequentially as usual.
355|
356|.. _opt-allow-parallel:
357|
358|You can also flip the default with ``--allow-parallel`` (or
359|``nox.options.allow_parallel = True`` in the Noxfile): every session then runs
360|concurrently unless it opts out with ``allow_parallel=False``. A session's own
361|``allow_parallel=`` value always wins over the global default, and
362|``--no-allow-parallel`` on the command line overrides the Noxfile setting.
363|This makes it easy to try ``--parallel`` on a Noxfile that hasn't declared
364|anything yet::
365|
366|    nox --parallel auto --allow-parallel
367|
368|Sessions are scheduled according to their dependencies: a session declared with
369|``requires=`` does not start until all of its prerequisites have completed
370|successfully, and is reported as ``aborted`` (and never started) if any
371|prerequisite fails. ``--stop-on-first-error`` stops launching new sessions after
372|the first failure; sessions already running are allowed to finish, and their
373|results still appear in the summary and in any ``--report`` file.
374|
375|Each session's output is buffered and printed as a single block when that
376|session finishes, so output from concurrent sessions never interleaves. On an
377|interactive terminal a live status board shows which sessions are currently
378|running.
379|
380|.. note::
381|
382|    Because each session runs in its own subprocess that reads only from a pipe,
383|    sessions cannot prompt for input under ``--parallel`` (``session.interactive``
384|    is ``False``). Dynamic session scheduling via ``session.notify`` is not
385|    supported in parallel mode and raises an error; use ``requires=`` to order
386|    sessions instead.
387|
388|
389|.. _opt-error-on-missing-interpreters:
390|
391|Failing sessions when the interpreter is missing
392|------------------------------------------------
393|
394|By default, when not on CI, Nox will skip sessions where the Python interpreter can't be found. If you want Nox to mark these sessions as failed, you can use ``--error-on-missing-interpreters``:
395|
396|.. code-block:: console
397|
398|    nox --error-on-missing-interpreters
399|
400|If the Noxfile sets ``nox.options.error_on_missing_interpreters``, you can override the Noxfile setting from the command line by using ``--no-error-on-missing-interpreters``.
401|
402|If being run on Continuous Integration (CI) systems, Nox will treat missing interpreters as errors by default to avoid sessions silently passing when the requested python interpreter is not installed. Nox does this by looking for an environment variable called ``CI`` which is a convention used by most CI providers.
403|
404|.. _opt-error-on-external-run:
405|
406|Disallowing external programs
407|-----------------------------
408|
409|By default Nox will warn but ultimately allow you to run programs not installed in the session's virtualenv. You can use ``--error-on-external-run`` to make Nox fail the session if it uses any external program without explicitly passing ``external=True`` into :func:`session.run <nox.sessions.Session.run>`:
410|
411|.. code-block:: console
412|
413|    nox --error-on-external-run
414|
415|Programs in sibling directories are still external, even when the directory names share a prefix with the virtualenv's binary directory.
416|
417|If the Noxfile sets ``nox.options.error_on_external_run``, you can override the Noxfile setting from the command line by using ``--no-error-on-external-run``.
418|
419|Specifying a different configuration file
420|-----------------------------------------
421|
422|If for some reason your Noxfile is not named *noxfile.py*, you can use ``--noxfile`` or ``-f``:
423|
424|.. code-block:: console
425|
426|    nox --noxfile something.py
427|    nox -f something.py
428|
429|
430|.. _opt-envdir:
431|
432|Storing virtualenvs in a different directory
433|--------------------------------------------
434|
435|By default Nox stores virtualenvs in ``./.nox``, however, you can change this using ``--envdir``:
436|
437|.. code-block:: console
438|
439|    nox --envdir /tmp/envs
440|
441|
442|Skipping everything but install commands
443|----------------------------------------
444|
445|There are a couple of cases where it makes sense to have Nox only run ``install`` commands, such as preparing an environment for offline testing or re-creating the same virtualenvs used for testing. You can use ``--install-only`` to skip ``run`` commands.
446|
447|For example, given this Noxfile:
448|
449|.. code-block:: python
450|
451|    @nox.session
452|    def tests(session):
453|        session.install("pytest")
454|        session.install(".")
455|        session.run("pytest")
456|
457|
458|Running:
459|
460|.. code-block:: console
461|
462|    nox --install-only
463|
464|
465|Would run both ``install`` commands, but skip the ``run`` command:
466|
467|.. code-block:: console
468|
469|    nox > Running session tests
470|    nox > Creating virtualenv using python3.12 in ./.nox/tests
471|    nox > python -m pip install pytest
472|    nox > python -m pip install .
473|    nox > Skipping pytest run, as --install-only is set.
474|    nox > Session tests was successful.
475|
476|
477|Forcing non-interactive behavior
478|--------------------------------
479|
480|:attr:`session.interactive <nox.sessions.Session.interactive>` can be used to tell if Nox is being run from an interactive terminal (such as an actual human running it on their computer) vs run in a non-interactive terminal (such as a continuous integration system).
481|
482|.. code-block:: python
483|
484|    @nox.session
485|    def docs(session):
486|        ...
487|
488|        if session.interactive:
489|            session.run("sphinx-autobuild", ...)
490|        else:
491|            session.run("sphinx-build", ...)
492|
493|Sometimes it's useful to force Nox to see the session as non-interactive. You can use the ``--non-interactive`` argument to do this:
494|
495|.. code-block:: bash
496|
497|    nox --non-interactive
498|
499|
500|This will cause ``session.interactive`` to always return ``False``.
501|
502|
503|Controlling color output
504|------------------------
505|
506|By default, Nox will output colorful logs if you're using it in an interactive
507|terminal. However, if you are redirecting ``stderr`` to a file or otherwise
508|not using an interactive terminal, or the environment variable ``NO_COLOR`` is
509|set, Nox will output in plaintext. If this is not set, and ``FORCE_COLOR`` is
510|present, color will be forced.
511|
512|You can manually control Nox's output using the ``--nocolor`` and ``--forcecolor`` flags.
513|
514|For example, this will always output colorful logs:
515|
516|.. code-block:: console
517|
518|    nox --forcecolor
519|
520|However, this will never output colorful logs:
521|
522|.. code-block:: console
523|
524|    nox --nocolor
525|
526|
527|.. _opt-verbose:
528|
529|
530|Controlling commands verbosity
531|------------------------------
532|
533|By default, Nox will only show output of commands that fail, or, when the commands get passed ``silent=False``.
534|By either passing ``--verbose`` to Nox or setting ``nox.options.verbose = True``, all output of all commands
535|run is shown, regardless of the silent argument.
536|
537|
538|.. _opt-report:
539|
540|
541|Outputting a machine-readable report
542|------------------------------------
543|
544|You can output a report in ``json`` format by specifying ``--report``:
545|
546|.. code-block:: console
547|
548|    nox --report status.json
549|
550|
551|Converting from tox
552|-------------------
553|
554|Nox has experimental support for converting ``tox.ini`` files into ``noxfile.py`` files. This doesn't support every feature of tox and is intended to just do most of the mechanical work of converting over- you'll likely still need to make a few changes to the converted ``noxfile.py``.
555|
556|To use the converter, install ``nox`` with the ``tox-to-nox`` extra:
557|
558|.. code-block:: console
559|
560|    pip install --upgrade nox[tox-to-nox]
561|
562|Then, just run ``tox-to-nox`` in the directory where your ``tox.ini`` resides:
563|
564|.. code-block:: console
565|
566|    tox-to-nox
567|
568|This will create a ``noxfile.py`` based on the environments in your ``tox.ini``. Some things to note:
569|
570|- `Generative environments`_ work, but will be converted as individual environments. ``tox-to-nox`` isn't quite smart enough to turn these into :ref:`parametrized <running_paramed_sessions>` sessions, but it should be straightforward to manually pull out common configuration for parametrization.
571|- Due to the way tox parses its configuration, all `substitutions`_ are baked in when converting. This means you'll need to replace the static strings in the ``noxfile.py`` with appropriate variables.
572|- Several non-common tox options aren't implemented, but it's possible to do so. Please file a feature request if you run into one you think will be useful.
573|
574|.. _Generative environments: http://tox.readthedocs.io/en/latest/config.html#generating-environments-conditional-settings
575|.. _substitutions: http://tox.readthedocs.io/en/latest/config.html#substitutions
576|
577|
578|Shell Completion
579|----------------
580|Add the appropriate command to your shell's config file
581|so that it is run on startup. You will likely have to restart
582|or re-login for the autocompletion to start working.
583|
584|bash
585|
586|.. code-block:: console
587|
588|    eval "$(register-python-argcomplete nox)"
589|
590|zsh
591|
592|.. code-block:: console
593|
594|    # To activate completions for zsh you need to have
595|    # bashcompinit enabled in zsh:
596|    autoload -U bashcompinit
597|    bashcompinit
598|
599|    # Afterwards you can enable completion for Nox:
600|    eval "$(register-python-argcomplete nox)"
601|
602|tcsh
603|
604|.. code-block:: console
605|
606|    eval `register-python-argcomplete --shell tcsh nox`
607|
608|fish
609|
610|.. code-block:: console
611|
612|    register-python-argcomplete --shell fish nox | .

1|Tutorial
2|========
3|
4|This tutorial will walk you through installing, configuring, and running Nox.
5|
6|
7|Installation
8|------------
9|
10|Nox can be easily installed via `pip`_:
11|
12|.. code-block:: console
13|
14|    python3 -m pip install nox
15|
16|You may want to use the `user site`_ to avoid messing with your global Python install:
17|
18|.. code-block:: console
19|
20|    python3 -m pip install --user nox
21|
22|Or you can be extra fancy and use `pipx`_:
23|
24|.. code-block:: console
25|
26|    pipx install nox
27|
28|Either way, Nox is usually installed *globally*, similar to ``tox``, ``pip``, and other similar tools.
29|
30|If you're interested in running ``nox`` within `docker`_, you can use the `thekevjames/nox images`_ on DockerHub which contain builds for all ``nox`` versions and all supported ``python`` versions. Nox is also supported via ``pipx run nox`` in the `manylinux images`_.
31|
32|If you want to run ``nox`` within `GitHub Actions`_, you can use the ``wntrblm/nox`` action, which installs the latest ``nox`` and makes available a default set of active CPython versions:
33|
34|.. code-block:: yaml
35|
36|    # setup nox with the default set of CPython versions i.e.
37|    # python-versions: "3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14, 3.15"
38|    # Any Nox tag will work here
39|    - uses: wntrblm/nox@2026.07.11
40|
41|    # setup nox only for a given list of python versions
42|    # Limitations:
43|    # - Version specifiers shall be supported by actions/setup-python
44|    # - There can only be one "major.minor" per interpreter i.e. "3.12.0, 3.12.1" is invalid
45|    # Any Nox tag will work here
46|    - uses: wntrblm/nox@2026.07.11
47|      with:
48|          python-versions: "3.10, 3.14, pypy-3.11"
49|
50|.. _pip: https://pip.readthedocs.org
51|.. _user site: https://packaging.python.org/tutorials/installing-packages/#installing-to-the-user-site
52|.. _pipx: https://packaging.python.org/guides/installing-stand-alone-command-line-tools/
53|.. _docker: https://www.docker.com/
54|.. _thekevjames/nox images: https://hub.docker.com/r/thekevjames/nox
55|.. _GitHub Actions: https://github.com/features/actions
56|.. _manylinux images: https://github.com/pypa/manylinux
57|
58|Writing the configuration file
59|------------------------------
60|
61|Nox is configured via a file called ``noxfile.py`` in your project's directory.
62|This file is a Python file that defines a set of *sessions*. A *session* is
63|an environment and a set of commands to run in that environment. If you're
64|familiar with tox sessions are analogous to *environments*. If you're familiar
65|with GNU Make, sessions are analogous to *targets*.
66|
67|Sessions are declared using the ``@nox.session`` decorator. This is similar to
68|how Flask uses ``@app.route``.
69|
70|Here's a basic Noxfile that runs `flake8`_ against ``example.py`` (you can create
71|``example.py`` yourself)::
72|
73|    import nox
74|
75|    @nox.session
76|    def lint(session):
77|        session.install("flake8")
78|        session.run("flake8", "example.py")
79|
80|.. _flake8: http://flake8.pycqa.org/en/latest/
81|
82|
83|Running Nox for the first time
84|------------------------------
85|
86|Now that you've installed Nox and have a Noxfile you can run Nox! Open your
87|project's directory in a terminal and run ``nox``. You should see something
88|like this:
89|
90|.. code-block:: console
91|
92|    $ nox
93|    nox > Running session lint
94|    nox > Creating virtualenv using python3.14 in .nox/lint
95|    nox > pip install flake8
96|    nox > flake8 example.py
97|    nox > Session lint was successful.
98|
99|
100|**✨ You've now successfully used Nox for the first time! ✨**
101|
102|The rest of this tutorial will take you through other common things you'll
103|likely want to do with Nox. You can also jump into :doc:`usage` and
104|:doc:`config` docs if you want.
105|
106|
107|Installing dependencies
108|-----------------------
109|
110|Nox more or less passes ``session.install`` through to ``pip``, so you can
111|install stuff in the usual way. Here's some examples:
112|
113|To install one or more packages at a time:
114|
115|.. code-block:: python
116|
117|    @nox.session
118|    def tests(session):
119|        # same as pip install pytest protobuf>3.0.0
120|        session.install("pytest", "protobuf>3.0.0")
121|        ...
122|
123|To install a ``requirements.txt`` file:
124|
125|.. code-block:: python
126|
127|    @nox.session
128|    def tests(session):
129|        # same as pip install -r requirements.txt
130|        session.install("-r", "requirements.txt")
131|        ...
132|
133|If your project is a Python package and you want to install it:
134|
135|.. code-block:: python
136|
137|    @nox.session
138|    def tests(session):
139|        # same as pip install .
140|        session.install(".")
141|        ...
142|
143|In some cases such as Python binary extensions, your package may depend on
144|code compiled outside of the Python ecosystem. To make sure a low-level
145|dependency (e.g. ``libfoo``) is available during installation:
146|
147|.. code-block:: python
148|
149|    @nox.session
150|    def tests(session):
151|        ...
152|        session.run_install(
153|            "cmake", "-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug",
154|            "-S", libfoo_src_dir,
155|            "-B", build_dir,
156|            external=True,
157|        )
158|        session.run_install(
159|            "cmake",
160|            "--build", build_dir,
161|            "--config", "Debug",
162|            "--target", "install",
163|            external=True,
164|        )
165|        session.install(".")
166|        ...
167|
168|These commands will run even if you are only installing, and will not run if
169|the environment is being reused without reinstallation.
170|
171|
172|Loading dependencies from pyproject.toml or scripts
173|---------------------------------------------------
174|
175|One common need is loading a dependency list from a ``pyproject.toml`` file
176|(say to prepare an environment without installing the package) or supporting
177|`PEP 723 <https://peps.python.org/pep-0723>`_ scripts. Nox provides a helper to
178|load these with ``nox.project.load_toml``. It can be passed a filepath to a toml
179|file or to a script file following PEP 723. For example, if you have the
180|following ``peps.py``:
181|
182|
183|.. code-block:: python
184|
185|    # /// script
186|    # requires-python = ">=3.11"
187|    # dependencies = [
188|    #   "requests<3",
189|    #   "rich",
190|    # ]
191|    # ///
192|
193|    import requests
194|    from rich.pretty import pprint
195|
196|    resp = requests.get("https://peps.python.org/api/peps.json")
197|    data = resp.json()
198|    pprint([(k, v["title"]) for k, v in data.items()][:10])
199|
200|You can make a session for it like this:
201|
202|.. code-block:: python
203|
204|   @nox.session
205|   def peps(session):
206|       requirements = nox.project.load_toml("peps.py")["dependencies"]
207|       session.install(*requirements)
208|       session.run("python", "peps.py")
209|
210|This is a common structure for scripts following this PEP, so a helper for it
211|is provided:
212|
213|.. code-block:: python
214|
215|   @nox.session
216|   def peps(session):
217|       session.install_and_run_script("peps.py")
218|
219|
220|Other helpers for ``pyproject.toml`` based projects are also available in
221|``nox.project``.
222|
223|Running commands
224|----------------
225|
226|The ``session.run`` function lets you run commands within the context of your
227|session's virtual environment. Here's a few examples:
228|
229|You can install and run Python tools:
230|
231|.. code-block:: python
232|
233|    @nox.session
234|    def tests(session):
235|        session.install("pytest")
236|        session.run("pytest")
237|
238|
239|If you want to pass more arguments to a program just add more arguments to ``run``:
240|
241|.. code-block:: python
242|
243|    @nox.session
244|    def tests(session):
245|        session.install("pytest")
246|        session.run("pytest", "-v", "tests")
247|
248|
249|You can also pass environment variables:
250|
251|.. code-block:: python
252|
253|    @nox.session
254|    def tests(session):
255|        session.install("pytest")
256|        session.run(
257|            "pytest",
258|            env={
259|                "FLASK_DEBUG": "1"
260|            }
261|        )
262|
263|See :func:`nox.sessions.Session.run` for more options and examples for running
264|programs.
265|
266|Selecting which sessions to run
267|-------------------------------
268|
269|Once you have multiple sessions in your Noxfile you'll notice that Nox will
270|run them all by default. While this is useful, it often useful to just run
271|one or two at a time. You can use the ``--sessions`` argument (or ``-s``) to
272|select which sessions to run. You can use the ``--list`` argument to show which
273|sessions are available and which will be run. Here's some examples:
274|
275|Here's a Noxfile with three sessions:
276|
277|.. code-block:: python
278|
279|    import nox
280|
281|    @nox.session
282|    def test(session):
283|        ...
284|
285|    @nox.session
286|    def lint(session):
287|        ...
288|
289|    @nox.session
290|    def docs(session):
291|        ...
292|
293|
294|If you just run ``nox --list`` you'll see that all sessions are selected:
295|
296|.. code-block:: console
297|
298|    Sessions defined in noxfile.py:
299|
300|    * test
301|    * lint
302|    * docs
303|
304|    sessions marked with * are selected,
305|    sessions marked with - are skipped.
306|
307|
308|If you run ``nox --list --sessions lint`` you'll see that only the lint session
309|is selected:
310|
311|.. code-block:: console
312|
313|    Sessions defined in noxfile.py:
314|
315|    - test
316|    * lint
317|    - docs
318|
319|    sessions marked with * are selected,
320|    sessions marked with - are skipped.
321|
322|
323|And if you run ``nox --sessions lint`` Nox will just run the lint session:
324|
325|.. code-block:: console
326|
327|    nox > Running session lint
328|    nox > Creating virtualenv using python3 in .nox/lint
329|    nox > ...
330|    nox > Session lint was successful.
331|
332|
333|In the Noxfile, you can specify a default set of sessions to run. If so, a plain
334|``nox`` call will only trigger certain sessions:
335|
336|.. code-block:: python
337|
338|    import nox
339|
340|    nox.options.sessions = ["lint", "test"]
341|
342|If you set this to an empty list, Nox will not run any sessions by default, and
343|will print a helpful message with the ``--list`` output when a user does not
344|specify a session to run.
345|
346|There are many more ways to select and run sessions! You can read more about
347|invoking Nox in :doc:`usage`.
348|
349|Queuing sessions
350|-----------------
351|
352|If you want to queue up (or "notify") another session from the current one, you
353|can use the ``session.notify`` function. Pass the session name string, the same
354|name you would use with ``nox --session``:
355|
356|.. code-block:: python
357|
358|    @nox.session
359|    def tests(session):
360|        session.install("pytest")
361|        session.run("pytest")
362|        # Here we queue up the test coverage session to run next
363|        session.notify("coverage")
364|
365|    @nox.session
366|    def coverage(session):
367|        session.install("coverage")
368|        session.run("coverage")
369|
370|You can queue up any session you want, not just test and coverage sessions, but this is a very commonly
371|used pattern.
372|
373|Now running ``nox --session tests`` will run the tests session and then the coverage session.
374|
375|You can also pass the notified session positional arguments:
376|
377|.. code-block:: python
378|
379|    @nox.session
380|    def prepare_thing(session):
381|        thing_path = "./path/to/thing"
382|        session.run("prepare", "thing", thing_path)
383|        session.notify("consume_thing", posargs=[thing_path])
384|
385|    @nox.session
386|    def consume_thing(session):
387|        # The 'consume' command has the arguments
388|        # sent to it from the 'prepare_thing' session
389|        session.run("consume", "thing", *session.posargs)
390|
391|Note that this will only have the desired effect if selecting sessions to run via the ``--session/-s`` flag. If you simply run ``nox``, all selected sessions will be run.
392|
393|Requiring sessions
394|------------------
395|
396|You can also request sessions be run before your session runs. This is done with the ``requires=`` keyword:
397|
398|
399|.. code-block:: python
400|
401|    @nox.session
402|    def tests(session):
403|        session.install("pytest")
404|        session.run("pytest")
405|
406|    @nox.session(requires=["tests"])
407|    def coverage(session):
408|        session.install("coverage")
409|        session.run("coverage")
410|
411|The required sessions will be stably topologically sorted and run. Parametrized
412|sessions are supported. You can also get the current Python version with
413|``{python}``, though arbitrary parametrizations are not supported.
414|
415|
416|.. code-block:: python
417|
418|    @nox.session(python=["3.10", "3.13"])
419|    def tests(session):
420|        session.install("pytest")
421|        session.run("pytest")
422|
423|    @nox.session(python=["3.10", "3.13"], requires=["tests-{python}"])
424|    def coverage(session):
425|        session.install("coverage")
426|        session.run("coverage")
427|
428|Testing against different and multiple Pythons
429|----------------------------------------------
430|
431|Many projects need to support either a specific version of Python or multiple
432|Python versions. You can have Nox run your session against multiple
433|interpreters by specifying ``python`` to ``@nox.session``. Here's some examples:
434|
435|If you want your session to specifically run against a single version of Python only:
436|
437|.. code-block:: python
438|
439|    @nox.session(python="3.12")
440|    def test(session):
441|        ...
442|
443|If you want your session to run against multiple versions of Python:
444|
445|.. code-block:: python
446|
447|    @nox.session(python=["3.10", "3.11", "3.12"])
448|    def test(session):
449|        ...
450|
451|You'll notice that running ``nox --list`` will show that this one session has
452|been expanded into three distinct sessions:
453|
454|.. code-block:: console
455|
456|    Sessions defined in noxfile.py:
457|
458|    * test-3.10
459|    * test-3.11
460|    * test-3.12
461|
462|You can run all of the ``test`` sessions using ``nox --sessions test`` or run
463|an individual one using the full name as displayed in the list, for example,
464|``nox --sessions test-3.12``. More details on selecting sessions can be found
465|over in the :doc:`usage` documentation.
466|
467|You can read more about configuring the virtual environment used by your
468|sessions over at :ref:`virtualenv config`.
469|
470|
471|Testing with conda
472|------------------
473|
474|Some projects, especially in the data science community, need to test that
475|they work in a conda environment. If you want your session to run in a conda
476|environment:
477|
478|.. code-block:: python
479|
480|    @nox.session(venv_backend="conda")
481|    def test(session):
482|        ...
483|
484|Install packages with conda:
485|
486|.. code-block:: python
487|
488|    session.conda_install("pytest", channels=["conda-forge"])
489|
490|It is possible to install packages with pip into the conda environment, but
491|it's a best practice to only install pip packages with the ``--no-deps`` option.
492|This prevents pip from breaking the conda environment by installing incompatible
493|versions of packages already installed with conda. You should always specify
494|channels for consistency; default channels can vary (and ``micromamba`` has none).
495|
496|.. code-block:: python
497|
498|    session.install("contexter", "--no-deps")
499|    session.install("-e", ".", "--no-deps")
500|
501|``"mamba"`` is also allowed as a choice for ``venv_backend``, which will
502|use/require `mamba <https://github.com/mamba-org/mamba>`_ instead of conda.
503|
504|``"micromamba"`` is also allowed as a choice for ``venv_backend``, which will
505|use/require `micromamba <https://mamba.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/micromamba.html#>`_
506|instead of conda.
507|
508|Parametrization
509|---------------
510|
511|Just like Nox can handle running against multiple interpreters, Nox can also
512|handle running your sessions with a list of different arguments using the
513|:func:`nox.parametrize` decorator.
514|
515|Here's a short example of using parametrization to test against two different
516|versions of Django:
517|
518|.. code-block:: python
519|
520|    @nox.session
521|    @nox.parametrize("django", ["1.9", "2.0"])
522|    def test(session, django):
523|        session.install(f"django=={django}")
524|        session.run("pytest")
525|
526|
527|If you run ``nox --list`` you'll see that Nox expands your one session into
528|multiple sessions. One for each argument value that you want to be passed to
529|your session:
530|
531|.. code-block:: console
532|
533|    Sessions defined in noxfile.py:
534|
535|    * test(django='1.9')
536|    * test(django='2.0')
537|
538|
539|:func:`nox.parametrize` has an interface and usage intentionally similar to
540|`pytest's parametrize`_. It's an extremely powerful feature of Nox. You can
541|read more about parametrization and see more examples over at
542|:ref:`parametrized`.
543|
544|.. _pytest's parametrize: https://pytest.org/latest/parametrize.html#_pytest.python.Metafunc.parametrize
545|
546|
547|.. _session tags:
548|
549|Session tags
550|------------
551|
552|You can add tags to your sessions to help you organize your development tasks:
553|
554|.. code-block:: python
555|
556|    @nox.session(tags=["style", "fix"])
557|    def black(session):
558|        session.install("black")
559|        session.run("black", "my_package")
560|
561|    @nox.session(tags=["style", "fix"])
562|    def isort(session):
563|        session.install("isort")
564|        session.run("isort", "my_package")
565|
566|    @nox.session(tags=["style"])
567|    def flake8(session):
568|        session.install("flake8")
569|        session.run("flake8", "my_package")
570|
571|
572|If you run ``nox -t style``, Nox will run all three sessions:
573|
574|.. code-block:: console
575|
576|    * black
577|    * isort
578|    * flake8
579|
580|
581|If you run ``nox -t fix``, Nox will only run the ``black`` and ``isort``
582|sessions:
583|
584|.. code-block:: console
585|
586|    * black
587|    * isort
588|    - flake8
589|
590|
591|If you run ``nox -t style fix``, Nox will run all sessions that match *any* of
592|the tags, so all three sessions:
593|
594|.. code-block:: console
595|
596|    * black
597|    * isort
598|    * flake8
599|
600|
601|Running without the nox command or adding dependencies
602|------------------------------------------------------
603|
604|With a few small additions to your noxfile, you can support running using only
605|a generalized Python runner, such as ``pipx run noxfile.py``, ``uv run
606|noxfile.py``, ``pdm run noxfile.py``, or ``hatch run noxfile.py``. You need to
607|have the following comment in your noxfile:
608|
609|.. code-block:: python
610|
611|   # /// script
612|   # dependencies = ["nox"]
613|   # ///
614|
615|And the following block of code:
616|
617|.. code-block:: python
618|
619|   if __name__ == "__main__":
620|       nox.main()
621|
622|If this comment block is present, nox will also read it, and run a custom
623|environment (``_nox_script_mode``) if the dependencies or ``requires-python``
624|are not met in the current environment. This allows you to specify
625|dependencies for your noxfile, a minimum version of nox, or a Python version
626|requirement here. If the running interpreter does not satisfy
627|``requires-python``, nox will find or download a matching Python for the
628|environment (controlled by ``--download-python``, ``NOX_SCRIPT_DOWNLOAD_PYTHON``,
629|or ``tool.nox.script-download-python``), and a reused environment is rebuilt
630|if its Python no longer qualifies. The ``none`` script backend cannot switch
631|interpreters, so a mismatch there is an error. If only ``requires-python``
632|is given, nox itself is the implied dependency. You can control this with
633|``--script-mode``/``NOX_SCRIPT_MODE``; ``none`` will deactivate it, and
634|``fresh`` will rebuild it; the default is ``reuse``. You can also set
635|``--script-venv-backend``/``tool.nox.script-venv-backend``/``NOX_SCRIPT_VENV_BACKEND``
636|to control the backend used; the default is ``"uv|virtualenv"``.
